pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** The Periodic Table

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'The Periodic Table'):** The principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; the Periodic Table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals; how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the Periodic Table; the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-1 / MS-PS1-2 supporting):** Use models and patterns in properties of substances; the periodic table organises elements by property patterns (framework PS1.A).

- **Operational details:** The big idea is ORGANISATION BY PATTERN: elements are arranged by increasing atomic number into GROUPS (columns — similar chemical behaviour) and PERIODS (rows), with metals to the left/centre and non-metals to the upper right. The table's power is PREDICTION — knowing an element's position predicts its properties and reactivity (e.g. Group 1 metals get more reactive down the group; Group 0 are unreactive). Teach Mendeleev's insight historically: he ordered by properties, left GAPS for undiscovered elements, and successfully PREDICTED their properties — the periodic law as a genuine predictive theory, not a lookup chart. Have pupils discover periodicity by arranging element cards by property and seeing the repeating pattern emerge. Emphasise position→property inference over memorising the whole table.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child locates metals/non-metals and a named group/period, uses position to predict a property or relative reactivity, and explains why Mendeleev's gaps-and-predictions made the table a scientific triumph.
bestPractices: Have pupils discover periodicity by arranging elements by property until the repeating pattern emerges, rather than presenting the finished table.
Teach position→property PREDICTION as the table's purpose, not memorisation of every element.
Tell the Mendeleev story concretely: ordering by properties, leaving gaps, predicting undiscovered elements.
Use group highlights to show trends (Group 1 more reactive down; Group 0 inert).
Distinguish groups (columns, similar chemistry) from periods (rows) explicitly.
keyRepresentations: Element cards with property tags to sort into the grid
The periodic table grid with group (column) and period (row) highlighters
commonMisconceptions: The periodic table is an arbitrary chart to memorise rather than an ordered predictive system.
Rows (periods) share properties, confusing them with groups (columns).
The table is ordered by atomic MASS in all cases (Mendeleev's a few anomalies; modern order is atomic number).
All metals are equally reactive (missing the group/position trends).
Elements were placed by discovery date rather than by properties.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 11–12 learn the periodic table as an organisation-by-pattern system whose power is PREDICTION, not memorisation. They discover periodicity by putting element cards in order (atomic weight as Mendeleev did, or atomic number as in the modern table) and starting new rows so similar properties line up until the repeating pattern emerges, use position (group/period) to predict properties and relative reactivity, and understand Mendeleev's historical insight of leaving gaps and predicting undiscovered elements. Core distinctions: groups (columns, similar chemistry; in the main groups, the same number of outer-shell electrons, with helium the exception in Group 0) versus periods (rows), and metals (left/centre) versus non-metals (upper right, plus hydrogen).

activities.title: Become Mendeleev: sort element cards until the pattern snaps into place
feedback: When sorting locks into place, point out that the repeat the pupil just produced IS periodicity — the same pattern Mendeleev spotted.

If a prediction for the gap is close, affirm that reading the neighbours' trend is precisely how the table predicts; if far off, prompt them to re-read the column above and below the gap before revealing the real element.
When highlighting Group 1, draw attention to reactivity increasing DOWN the column; when highlighting Group 0, that these elements stay unreactive — position predicts behaviour.
If a pupil groups cards by an incidental feature (such as colour or appearance) rather than chemical property, prompt them to compare how two column-mates actually REACT.
activities.rationale: The periodic law is a discovery about pattern and prediction, intended to be grasped by re-enacting Mendeleev's move: order elements (he used atomic weight) and arrange them so similar properties line up until the repeat emerges, leave a gap, predict the missing element. Doing the sorting and committing to a prediction before the reveal is intended to make periodicity a felt insight and to foreground position→property inference over rote memorisation. Dragging, locking-on-correct-order, group/period highlighters and tap-to-reveal property panels are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; periods and groups; metals and non-metals; predicting patterns in reactions from the Periodic Table
The periodic table organises elements by patterns in properties; position predicts behaviour (NGSS PS1.A / MS-PS1-1 models and patterns)
Mendeleev left gaps and successfully predicted undiscovered elements' properties, demonstrating the periodic law's predictive power
learnerActions: Receive a shuffled set of element cards, each showing the element's atomic weight (or atomic number) and a few properties (e.g. reactivity, metal/non-metal, how it bonds).
Put the cards in order of atomic weight (or atomic number), starting a new row whenever properties begin to repeat, so that similar elements line up into columns.
Notice the moment when rows and columns align and a repeating pattern (periodicity) emerges from your own sorting rather than being handed to you.
Encounter a gap — one square that stays empty — and PREDICT the missing element's properties from its neighbours above, below, and beside it.
Commit to your prediction, then reveal the real element Mendeleev foretold and compare it against what you predicted.
Use group and period highlighters to trace Group 1 reactivity climbing down the column and Group 0 sitting inert, then tap any element to read its property panel.
activities.intendedInsight: The periodic table is a predictive law, not a chart to memorise: arranging elements so repeating property patterns fall into columns (the modern table orders by atomic number; Mendeleev ordered largely by atomic weight) means an element's POSITION lets you predict its properties and reactivity. It is this pattern-reasoning — not any particular ordering basis — that let Mendeleev leave gaps and foretell undiscovered elements.

activities.title: Tap-a-group reference table: reveal shared trends
feedback: When a group is highlighted, name the shared trait the members have in common so the highlight is tied to a reason, not just colour.
If a pupil treats a row as sharing properties, contrast it with a highlighted column to show where similar chemistry actually lies.
activities.rationale: A tappable, group-highlighting table is a useful reference and a clear shared-attribute reveal. It is offered as a companion to, not a replacement for, the sorting discovery: a fixed reference table shows the finished pattern and shared-attribute highlights well, but on its own it does not require the pupil to arrange and predict, which is what explains why the table is predictive.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; periods and groups; metals and non-metals; predicting patterns in reactions from the Periodic Table
The periodic table organises elements by patterns in properties; position predicts behaviour (NGSS PS1.A / MS-PS1-1 models and patterns)
learnerActions: Use a tappable periodic table where tapping a group highlights all its members and reveals their shared chemical trend.
Tap a group (e.g. Group 1) to see every member highlighted, then read the shared property that unites the column.
Compare tapping down a GROUP (column) against tracing across a PERIOD (row) to feel how the two directions differ.

Locate metals, non-metals and metalloids and notice they occupy a pattern (metals left/centre, non-metals upper-right, metalloids along the dividing staircase, with hydrogen a non-metal exception at top left), not scattered positions.
activities.intendedInsight: Column-mates (a group) share chemical behaviour because they share the same number of outer-shell electrons, and tapping a group makes this shared attribute visible at a glance; this serves as an ongoing reference once the arrange-and-predict discovery has established WHY the table is powerful.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: Group 1 reactivity down the column
feedback: If the prediction has no stated reason, press for WHY using the group trend before observing.
A correct prediction of a fiercer sodium reaction, justified by position in Group 1, is full credit; observing confirms it.
If the pupil predicts by atom size or weight 'look' alone, redirect to the shared chemical behaviour of the group.
activities.rationale: Predict-Observe-Explain makes the predictive claim testable and exposes whether the pupil is using the pattern or treating the table as an arbitrary list. The spoken/written reason, not just the prediction, reveals understanding. Where real reactions cannot be shown safely, a clip or recorded demonstration stands in; the represented reaction, not the medium, carries the learning.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; periods and groups; metals and non-metals; predicting patterns in reactions from the Periodic Table
Mendeleev left gaps and successfully predicted undiscovered elements' properties, demonstrating the periodic law's predictive power
learnerActions: Watch a short clip or records of lithium reacting with water.
Before observing, PREDICT what sodium (the next element down Group 1) will do and state WHY, referring to the group pattern.
Observe sodium's reaction and compare it with your prediction.
Explain the result: elements lower in Group 1 react more vigorously, and say how position in the table let you predict this.
Extend: without looking it up, predict how rubidium (the element below potassium in Group 1) would react with water, and give your reason before seeing any evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the group pattern lets you predict reactivity before observing: a pupil who sees the table as a mere list cannot predict, while one who reads the Group 1 trend predicts a more vigorous reaction further down the column — the stated reason is the diagnostic part.

activities.title: Explain the layout: why these elements share a column
feedback: Full credit links 'same group = similar properties' to the arrangement by atomic number, not just the fact on its own.

If a pupil explains column-mates by an incidental feature (similar size or weight), correct: it is ordered by atomic number so shared chemical behaviour lines up in columns — show Group 1 metals all reacting in a similar way with water, more vigorously further down.
If groups and periods are mixed up, state: columns = groups = similar chemistry; rows = periods = one shell filling across — then trace Group 1 down and Period 2 across.

If Mendeleev is credited with discovering or inventing elements, correct: he ordered KNOWN elements (largely by atomic weight) by pattern, left gaps where the pattern demanded an undiscovered element, and predicted its properties, later confirmed.
activities.rationale: Articulating why column-mates belong together distinguishes a pupil who grasps the table as a pattern of properties from one who thinks it is alphabetical, size-ordered or arbitrary. The Mendeleev gaps-and-prediction story only makes sense to the former, so requiring an explanation (not recognition) targets the core conceptual distinction and the common misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; periods and groups; metals and non-metals; predicting patterns in reactions from the Periodic Table
Mendeleev left gaps and successfully predicted undiscovered elements' properties, demonstrating the periodic law's predictive power
learnerActions: Consider that lithium, sodium and potassium sit in the same COLUMN (Group 1) but are not next to each other in the element counting order.
Explain why the table puts them together in one column — what they share and why that is more useful than listing elements in order.
State explicitly the difference between going DOWN a group and going ACROSS a period.
Say why Mendeleev left empty spaces instead of filling positions in order, and why those gaps mattered.
Describe where metals and non-metals are found — in a pattern, not scattered.
activities.intendedInsight: Elements in the same group share chemical properties because they have the same number of outer-shell electrons; ordering by atomic number arranges the table so these repeating patterns line up in columns, which is what makes it predictive rather than a mere list — and why Mendeleev's gaps-and-predictions were a scientific triumph.

activities.title: Optional enrichment: interview Mendeleev
feedback: Steer the conversation back to the pattern-and-prediction reasoning if it drifts into unrelated biography.
Reinforce that the gaps were a prediction the pattern DEMANDED, later confirmed by discovery.
activities.rationale: An in-role chat can vividly convey the historical daring of leaving gaps and predicting elements. It is offered as optional enrichment: a conversation conveys the story and motivation but does not let the pupil manipulate the arrangement or verify a prediction, so it complements rather than replaces the hands-on sorting and prediction work.
sourceClaims: Mendeleev left gaps and successfully predicted undiscovered elements' properties, demonstrating the periodic law's predictive power
learnerActions: Take part in an in-role conversation interviewing Mendeleev about his table.
Ask why he trusted the pattern enough to leave gaps rather than simply placing the next-heaviest known element in every position.
Draw out how he predicted the properties of elements not yet discovered, and how confirmation later vindicated him.
activities.intendedInsight: Mendeleev's daring was spotting a property pattern and trusting it enough to predict undiscovered elements — history that dramatises why the periodic law is a genuine predictive theory, not a lookup chart.

constraints: Target the big idea 'organisation by pattern → prediction': teach position→property inference, not memorisation of every element.
Distinguish groups (columns, similar chemistry, same outer-shell electron count) from periods (rows, one shell filling across) explicitly; do not let them be treated as interchangeable.

The modern table is ordered by atomic NUMBER, not atomic mass; Mendeleev ordered largely by atomic weight and had a few anomalies. Keep these distinct when telling the history, including in any activity insight.
Credit Mendeleev with spotting the pattern, leaving gaps, and predicting undiscovered elements' properties — not with discovering or inventing the elements.

A tappable reference table and the Mendeleev conversation are companions/enrichment: they show or narrate the pattern but do not by themselves require the pupil to arrange elements and commit to a prediction, which is where the discovery of WHY the table predicts occurs. Do not assert that any one medium is the only or best way to teach this.

Recognition or tap-to-highlight responses alone do not elicit the independent explanation (linking shared group properties to atomic-number arrangement) or the independent prediction that evidence the full response level; include construction/explanation tasks.
Handle reactive-metal demonstrations safely: use a clip or recorded records of alkali-metal reactions rather than unsupervised practical work with sodium/potassium.
Reactivity increases DOWN Group 1 and Group 0 elements are unreactive; keep trend directions accurate when using highlighters or predictions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, only the DfE KS3 programmes of study is marked verified in the source row; the NGSS and Royal Society of Chemistry claims are marked unverified. Do not treat citations as evidence that any activity here was tested or is comparatively more effective.

The original row's 3D-interactive entry was rated 'poor' with the claim that 3D 'adds no spatial meaning and obscures the row/column patterns'. This is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it is recorded here and in the audit but not asserted as universal — a 2D grid simply suits the row/column organisation that carries this concept.

The original 'static art cannot deliver the arrange-and-predict discovery' phrasing has been softened: a fixed reference table can still teach shared-attribute recognition; it simply does not itself require the pupil to arrange and predict.

Candidate activity 2's intendedInsight originally claimed tap-a-group was 'the quickest way to see group identity'; this unsupported comparative efficacy claim was removed and replaced with a narrow 'visible at a glance' affordance.

In this review, activity 1's intendedInsight was corrected: it previously implied Mendeleev ordered by atomic number. The evidence row and pedagogy state Mendeleev ordered largely by atomic weight while the modern table orders by atomic number; the insight now distinguishes the two and attributes the gap-prediction to pattern-reasoning rather than a specific ordering basis.
Activity 1's rationale previously asserted the law is 'best grasped by' re-enacting Mendeleev's move; this untested comparative efficacy claim was softened to intended/proposed wording.

The source material conflates 'ordered by atomic number' (modern) with Mendeleev's ordering 'by atomic weight'. The evidence list even states Mendeleev 'ordered elements by atomic weight'. Both are kept but clearly distinguished in constraints and activities to avoid teaching that the modern table is mass-ordered.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: show a short clip/records of lithium reacting with water, then ask the child to PREDICT what sodium (next down Group 1) will do and WHY, before observing it. A child who sees the table as a mere list can't predict; a child who reads the group pattern predicts a more vigorous version. Observing sodium's fiercer reaction tests the prediction; the stated reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If a brand-new element were discovered and it sat under potassium in Group 1, what could you predict about how it reacts — before testing it?
What's the difference between going DOWN a group and going ACROSS a period?
Why did Mendeleev leave empty spaces in his table instead of filling them in order?
Where are the metals and non-metals found on the table — scattered, or in a pattern?
assess.correctAnswer: Elements in the same group/column have SIMILAR CHEMICAL PROPERTIES (Group 1 metals all react vigorously with water, form similar compounds) because they have the same number of outer-shell electrons. The table is arranged so that ordering by atomic number makes these repeating patterns line up in columns — that's what makes it predictive, not just a list. Full marks link 'same group = similar properties' to the arrangement.

errorPatterns.pattern: the table is ordered alphabetically or by how heavy/big the atoms look
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's ordered by atomic number, arranged so repeating property patterns fall into columns. Show that Group 1 all react the same way — the point is behaviour, not size or spelling.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because they're similar sizes or weights, so they end up near each other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains column-mates by an incidental feature, not shared chemical properties

errorPatterns.pattern: groups (columns) and periods (rows) are interchangeable / mixed up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Columns = groups = similar chemistry; rows = periods = one shell filling across. Trace Group 1 down and Period 2 across to feel the difference.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because they're in the same period, and periods all behave alike.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says elements in a ROW share properties, or uses 'group' for a period

errorPatterns.pattern: Mendeleev's genius was inventing the elements or finishing the table, not predicting from gaps
errorPatterns.nextMove: He ordered known elements by pattern, left GAPS where the pattern demanded an undiscovered element, and predicted its properties — later confirmed. That's the power of the pattern.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: credits Mendeleev with discovering elements rather than spotting the pattern and predicting missing ones

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the table is alphabetical/size-ordered or arbitrary; can't say what column-mates share; mixes up groups and periods.
responseLevels.full: Explains groups share chemical properties (outer electrons), that ordering by atomic number lines the patterns into columns, distinguishes groups from periods, and uses the pattern to predict — grasping why Mendeleev's gaps mattered.
responseLevels.partial: States 'same group = similar properties' but can't connect it to the arrangement/atomic-number ordering or use it to predict an unknown element — the fact without its predictive power.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lithium, sodium and potassium all sit in the same COLUMN (Group 1) of the periodic table. They aren't next to each other in the counting order of the elements. Why does the table put them together in one column — what do they share, and why is that more useful than just listing elements in order?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason distinguishes a child who grasps the table as a PATTERN of properties (groups share behaviour; the layout predicts) from one who thinks it's an arbitrary or alphabetical/size list. Mendeleev's leaving gaps to predict undiscovered elements only makes sense to the former.
